Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

emotion noun

also emotions, feeling, feelings, passion

classical

Cic. Off. 1.136 (Lewis & Short): mōtūs animī nimiī
Traupman 152
M-O s.v. emotion

animī mōtus, animī mōtūs m.

emotion, a stirring of the mind

Cicero’s plain expression, neither good nor bad; in the plural, animī mōtūs, the emotions. Traupman: animī mōtūs exprimere, to express one’s emotions.

Other words

  • affectus, affectūs m. — feeling, emotion; state of mind

    noun, fourth declension · also used · classical · Quīnt. 6.2.8 (Lewis & Short): adfectuum duae sunt speciēs; Phaedr. 3 prol. 33–37: affectūs propriōs in fābellās trānstulit; Traupman 152, 156

    In Cicero a state or disposition of mind; the sense “emotion, passion” is Quintilian’s and later prose’s, and in the post-Augustan writers it is often fondness, love (Lewis & Short).

  • perturbātiō, perturbātiōnis f. — passion, disturbing emotion

    noun, third declension · also used · classical · Cic. Off. 1.136 (Lewis & Short, s.v. mōtus); M-O s.v. emotion

    Cicero’s word for the Stoics’ πάθη, the emotions that unsettle the mind: grief, fear, desire, joy out of measure. So not a neutral word for a feeling; elsewhere it is confusion, disorder (Lewis & Short).

Examples

  • servitūs obnoxia, quia quae volēbat nōn audēbat dīcere, affectūs propriōs in fābellās trānstulit

    the slave, who did not dare say what he wanted, put his own feelings into fablesPhaedr. 3 prol. 33–37

  • circā movendōs adfectūs in hoc posita est, ut moveāmur ipsī

    the secret of stirring the emotions lies in being moved ourselvesQuīnt. 6.2.26

See also emotional, affect, excite, feel.
